title: Alokito Teacher Core
headline: Designing a training platform for four different roles
summary: I redesigned Alokito Teacher’s website and training experience, bringing teacher learning, institute enrollment, and training management into one shared design system.
coverAlt: Three Alokito Teachers screens on a maroon field — job search with live vacancy counts, the join-us homepage, and the employer hiring page

chapters.heading: One platform, different responsibilities
chapters.lead:
The existing homepage was outdated. The team needed a unified website that explained its courses, plans, and job platform.

The harder problem was behind the homepage. Teachers needed a learning path, institutes needed enrollment and progress views, and trainers and admins needed to manage assessments, content, and records.

I had to keep those responsibilities distinct while working through access rules, enrollment limits, and assessment logic.

chapters.heading: Map the rules before the screens
chapters.lead:
I reviewed local education, training, and job platforms, then worked with the client to turn the requirements into flows for each role.

I started with signup, the initial assessment, and the four-phase teacher journey. From there, I mapped the enrollment and management work around it.

I built the initial design system before exploring homepage variations, giving courses, plans, and the two job-platform audiences clear routes into the product.

images.alt: Alokito homepage with courses, teacher and recruiter routes, badges, and plans
images.caption: Courses, plans, and job opportunities have clear routes from the homepage.

chapters.heading: Build the patterns that new screens can grow from
chapters.lead:
With four dashboard roles and a growing set of flows, consistency needed to come from reusable parts.

I defined colour scales and a text hierarchy, then built buttons, inputs, form controls, tables, navigation, and progress indicators. These became the foundation for learning cards, enrollment summaries, and assessment questions.

images.alt: Alokito design-system colour scales for primary, secondary, and feedback colours
images.label: Colour scales

images.alt: Alokito type hierarchy with display, heading, paragraph, and caption styles
images.label: Text hierarchy

chapters.heading: Define the interaction states as well
chapters.lead:
Buttons included default, hover, focus, and disabled states. Inputs covered typing, validation, and read-only states.

Defining those states gave developers a clearer specification for what happens during use, alongside the full-experience prototype.

images.alt: Primary button variants in two sizes, with default, hover, focus, and disabled states
images.caption: Button sizes, icon positions, and interaction states.

chapters.heading: Validation belongs in the component
chapters.lead: The same input pattern supports filled, successful, and error states, keeping feedback consistent across the longer forms.

images.alt: Filled input component
images.label: Filled

images.alt: Input with success feedback
images.label: Success

images.alt: Input with error feedback
images.label: Error

chapters.heading: Explain what is available and what comes next
chapters.lead:
The program combines online courses, offline workshops, and assessments across four phases, with plan-based access to later phases.

I made the initial assessment the starting dashboard’s primary action. Once training begins, the dashboard shows the active phase, overall progress, and individual course states.

images.alt: Initial teacher dashboard prompting completion of the assessment
images.label: Starting point

images.alt: Teacher dashboard with phase progress, active courses, and locked later activities
images.label: Training in progress

chapters.heading: A lock needs an explanation
chapters.lead: Some activities depend on earlier work. The locked card explains the prerequisite, while later phases remain visible so teachers can see the path ahead.

images.alt: Available course card with progress and status
images.label: Available

images.alt: Locked course card explaining that the previous course must be completed
images.label: Prerequisite required

chapters.heading: Connect the score to the work behind it
chapters.lead:
I paired the final score with phase-level and activity-level breakdowns, keeping the result connected to courses, assignments, and workshops.

The wider program links training with certification and a profile teachers can use when applying for jobs.

images.alt: Anonymous phase report listing course, assignment, and workshop scores
images.caption: A phase result with the activity scores behind it.

chapters.heading: Put capacity beside the enrollment decision
chapters.lead:
Institute enrollment depends on purchased seats. I placed the current plan and remaining capacity above the teacher list, alongside distinct enrollment, pending, review, and rejected states.

Plans and billing have their own view for teacher quantities, additional capacity, purchase history, and invoices.

images.alt: Institute plan summary displaying remaining teacher enrollment capacity
images.caption: Remaining capacity stays visible before enrollment decisions.

images.alt: Institute plans and billing with teacher quantity, per-teacher plans, and purchase history
images.caption: Purchasing capacity and finding invoices have their own space.

chapters.heading: Make a complex form manageable to create
chapters.lead:
The assessment builder needed multiple question types, editable options, helper text, and required or optional fields.

I organized it around individual questions. The selected question opens for editing while the rest of the form remains visible. Reusable types cover text responses, multiple choice, ratings, video, and links.

images.alt: Assessment builder with editable question titles, helper text, options, and required toggles
images.caption: Configure one question while keeping the rest of the form in view.

chapters.heading: Keep the structure across screen sizes
chapters.lead:
I designed desktop and mobile versions and prototyped the full experience. Progress and prerequisite messages remain visible as cards and summaries stack vertically.

Trainers and admins also have searchable, filterable views for moving from an overview into records, reports, and phase content. I worked closely with two developers to hand over the designs and connected flows.

images.alt: Mobile teacher dashboard with assessment status, progress, and training cards
images.label: Teacher

images.alt: Mobile institute billing with plan quantity and purchase history
images.label: Institute

chapters.heading: Live, well received, and followed by further funding
chapters.lead:
The website and training platform are now live. The client loved the final experience. After development, Alokito raised funding to support further scaling.

My contribution covered the shared design system, role-specific flows, responsive interfaces, full-experience prototype, and close handoff with two developers.

The work made the program’s rules visible: what to complete next, why an activity is locked, how many seats remain, and what contributes to a teacher’s score.

title: Alokito Job Portal
duration: 2025 · Part of the 6–8 month Alokito project
headline: Designing both sides of teacher recruitment
summary: I designed Alokito’s job portal for educators finding work and schools hiring, connecting discovery, applications, job posting, and candidate review.
coverAlt: Alokito job search with keyword and location controls, filters, and teaching roles

chapters.heading: Connect two journeys with different decisions
chapters.lead:
Teachers need to decide whether a role fits, prepare their information, and follow an application. Recruiters need to define a role, compare candidates, and manage decisions.

The complexity was in the transitions: an incomplete profile before applying, a long form before publishing, and a candidate list before a detailed review.

I designed separate working spaces, connected through the same posting and application journey.

chapters.heading: Work through the paths and their exceptions
chapters.lead:
The portal grew out of the wider platform requirements and my review of local education and job websites.

I mapped the applicant journey from search to submission, including saved jobs, incomplete profiles, and withdrawal. For recruiters, I worked through posting, requirements, matching setup, and review.

I prototyped the complete experience so handoff could communicate the states between the main steps.

chapters.heading: The applicant journey
Extend the shared system around hiring
chapters.lead:
I built the wider platform’s design system first, then extended it for recruitment.

Job-card variants cover featured and standard listings, plus default and applied states on desktop and mobile. A reusable step component distinguishes not-started, active, and completed steps. Shared form and table patterns support the longer workflows.

images.alt: Job-card variants for featured and standard listings in default and applied states
images.caption: One job-card pattern supports listing and application states.

images.alt: Job-posting step component in not-started, active, and completed states
images.caption: The step pattern makes workflow progress visible.

chapters.heading: Help teachers judge the role before opening it
chapters.lead:
Search supports job titles, keywords, schools, and location, with filters for experience, employment type, work arrangement, and salary.

Result cards bring requirements and deadlines into the list. Teachers can save an opportunity or open the details for responsibilities, qualifications, skills, and school information.

images.alt: Teaching-job search with filters and result cards showing requirements and deadlines
images.label: Search

images.alt: Teaching-role details with qualifications, responsibilities, skills, and institute information
images.label: Review the role

chapters.heading: Make profile readiness actionable
chapters.lead:
An incomplete profile needed more than a percentage. I showed readiness on the dashboard and again during the application.

The warning names the missing sections and gives a direct action to complete the profile. The form also shows the application allowance and collects expected salary, turning readiness into a specific task.

images.alt: Profile warning naming missing training, accomplishments, and references with a Complete Profile action
images.caption: Name what is missing, then give a direct next step.

chapters.heading: Confirm submission and explain withdrawal
chapters.lead:
The completion screen confirms submission and explains the next steps, with routes back to the dashboard or more jobs.

I also designed a confirmed undo action. Its message explains that withdrawing means applying again. Applied, in-review, and saved jobs remain distinct on the dashboard.

images.alt: Application submission confirmation with next steps and navigation actions
images.caption: Submission has a clear completion state.

images.alt: Confirmation modal explaining that withdrawing an application requires reapplying
images.caption: Withdrawal is deliberate, with its consequence explained.

chapters.heading: Give a long posting form a clear structure
chapters.lead:
I divided posting into four steps: job details, candidate requirements, matching and restrictions, and payment and billing.

The step indicator keeps the sequence visible. Previous-step and save-for-later actions support review or a pause.

images.alt: Candidate requirements step with education, experience, skills, and badge criteria
images.caption: Group candidate requirements into a dedicated step.

chapters.heading: Make missing criteria visible before publishing
chapters.lead: The matching view distinguishes supplied and missing criteria. A missing skill criterion has its own action to add it, so the recruiter can address the gap within the flow.

images.alt: Matching setup identifying supplied criteria and a missing skill criterion
images.caption: Incomplete setup becomes a visible action.

chapters.heading: Move from the list to an informed review
chapters.lead:
The recruiter dashboard separates active, pending-approval, and rejected posts. Each job opens its own context and applicants.

I separated shortlisted candidates from the complete list, with search, filters, match scores, and status labels. A profile then reveals the detailed information behind the row before accept or reject actions.

images.alt: Recruiter dashboard with job-posting counts and active, pending, and rejected status tabs
images.caption: Job-posting states and applicant counts stay connected.

images.alt: Recruiter job summary showing applicant count, days remaining, and average match score
images.caption: Review begins with the context of the job.

chapters.heading: Reusable sections organize the candidate record
chapters.lead: Consistent profile sections give education, experience, training, and skills a shared structure. The list supports comparison; the profile supports a closer decision.

images.alt: Reusable profile-summary component patterns with headings and labelled information
images.caption: Profile-section patterns used to organize candidate information.

chapters.heading: Keep the journey usable across layouts
chapters.lead:
The mobile applicant dashboard retains profile completion, application summaries, discovery, and recent applications. Job search has its own mobile design.

I designed and prototyped the full experience, then worked closely with the same two developers on handoff.

images.alt: Mobile applicant dashboard with profile readiness, job summaries, and recent applications
images.label: Dashboard

images.alt: Mobile job search with stacked result cards and filters
images.label: Search

chapters.heading: A live portal within a growing platform
chapters.lead:
The applicant and recruiter experiences are now live. The client loved the delivered experience, and the wider Alokito platform raised funding after development to support further scaling.

My work covered the connected flows, recruitment components, responsive screens, full prototype, and developer handoff.

The strongest part of the design was making the transitions clear: from a result to a decision, from missing information to a ready application, and from a candidate list to a detailed review.

title: TaxRise
headline: Rebranding a high-intent website and simplifying the path to conversion
summary: TaxRise refreshed its brand. The website hadn't caught up, and people weren't reaching the lead form. I led the design direction with two junior designers.
coverAlt: Three TaxRise screens on a blue field — a customer stories feature, the executive team page, and a featured blog post on tax relief programs
galleryAlt: TaxRise homepage with a 'Let's resolve your tax issues' hero and a client results section, shown on desktop and mobile
Before and after comparison of the TaxRise free consultation page — the dense old layout beside the redesigned version with a clearer form and an expectations section
TaxRise customer stories page on mobile, beside a full story about a $206,000 IRS liability settled for $650
Team page on mobile showing the executive team, beside enrolled agent profiles with case counts
Angled view of mobile screens — tax relief services, blog listing, and about page

chapters.heading: The brand had moved forward. The website hadn't.
chapters.lead:
Pages built at different times used different layouts, different components, different calls to action. One company, several ways of doing the same thing.

People weren't making it from the site into the lead form either. That was the part the business cared about.

I led the design direction with two junior designers — the system, the key flows, the lead form, and the reviews that kept the rest consistent.

Three things had to happen:

images.pendingLabel: The four landing directions, side by side
images.alt: Four TaxRise landing page directions side by side, labelled v1 to v4 — a light compact layout, a dark blue hero, a green gradient hero and a light gradient hero
images.caption: Four full landing directions. The same sections in each — what moved was the arrangement, and the weight given to proof.

chapters.heading: From brand refresh to scalable system
chapters.lead:
Stakeholder requirements, visual research, mood boards. Then we went wide on direction.

I started with the structure. Once that settled, the visual system went around it — and the finished homepage became the foundation for everything else.

chapters.heading: Designed as a system, not a collection of pages
chapters.lead: The homepage settled the arguments. After that, 20+ pages: templates for the shapes that repeat, custom layouts where the content needed something else.

images.label: Typography
images.alt: TaxRise design system typography sheet — headings H1 to H6 from 64 down to 24, and paragraph sizes XXL to S, each in bold, medium and regular
images.caption: One scale for headings, one for paragraphs, with the weights fixed per size.

images.label: Colour
images.alt: TaxRise design system colour sheet — primary, gray, red, green and white, each in three steps with hex values
images.caption: Every swatch carries its hex, so nothing has to be eyedropped later.

images.label: Button
images.alt: TaxRise design system button sheet — filled, white, ghost and outline buttons in default, hover and disabled states

images.label: Accordion
images.alt: TaxRise design system accordion sheet — collapsed and expanded question rows, and a two-column FAQ variant

images.label: Card
images.alt: TaxRise design system card sheet — cards with and without icons, in resting and raised states

chapters.note: Every state drawn once, so a page is composed rather than redrawn.

images.label: Reusable page pattern
images.alt: Angled view of TaxRise mobile screens — a customer story, tax relief services, the blog listing and the about page

images.label: Content-heavy page
images.alt: TaxRise team page on mobile showing the executive team, beside enrolled agent profiles with case counts

chapters.heading: Turning intent into action
chapters.lead:
The form was where the journey paid off or ended. So I mapped it before I designed it.

Two answers change the path. Not sure which tax years are unfiled? The question gets skipped rather than guessed at. In bankruptcy? The form says so and offers a way back, instead of collecting details it can't act on.

images.alt: Before and after of the TaxRise free consultation page — the dense original beside the redesigned version
images.caption: The free consultation page, before and after — the front door to the form.

images.alt: User flow diagram for the TaxRise lead form — start, reasons for seeking relief, an unfiled-years decision with yes, no and not-sure paths, tax debt, federal or state, issue type, then a bankruptcy decision splitting into a wait-and-return ending and a qualified-and-schedule ending
images.caption: The flow, mapped and reviewed with stakeholders before any of the interface existed. The bankruptcy question splits it into two endings.

images.label: Entry
images.alt: TaxRise lead form entry screen — 'Interested in tax relief?' with a Get Started button, beside a panel showing a Trustpilot rating and BBB, NAEA and NATP accreditations
images.caption: Proof sits beside the form and stays there for every step.

images.label: Question
images.alt: TaxRise lead form question — 'Which tax years are unfiled?' with year checkboxes in two columns and a 'Not sure' option, under a progress bar
images.caption: One question per screen, a progress bar, and a way to say 'Not sure'.

images.label: Branch
images.alt: TaxRise lead form question — 'When do you expect your bankruptcy to discharge?' with month ranges and a 'Not Sure' option
images.caption: The branching question. The answer decides which ending someone gets.

images.label: Completion
images.alt: TaxRise lead form completion screen — 'Thank you, David!' with a message that a call is coming and a Schedule Appointment button
images.caption: The proof panel drops away. The screen's only job now is to say what happens next.

chapters.heading: The final experience

images.alt: TaxRise homepage — a 'Let's resolve your tax issues' hero, a client results section, the two-phase resolution process and the FAQ
images.caption: The homepage the rest of the site was built from.

images.alt: TaxRise customer stories page on mobile, beside a full story about a $206,000 IRS liability settled for $650
images.caption: Extending the system across content-heavy pages.

chapters.heading: A more cohesive experience with a stronger path to conversion
chapters.lead: Six to twelve months of design, review and iteration. Then handoff. After launch, Google Analytics showed more people reaching the lead form than before.
chapters.note:
A redesign is easy to mistake for a visual problem. The useful work was connecting brand, experience and conversion so they stopped pulling in different directions.

And designing the system before the screens. Small team, 20+ pages — the foundation is what let it scale.

title: ZO Skin Centre
summary: Four locations. Four separate websites. I restructured the platform around what people are deciding — a treatment, a practitioner, a place — not around which clinic owns the page.
coverAlt: Three ZO Skin Centre mobile screens on a blue field — the homepage with its locations list, Zein Obagi's practitioner profile, and the Beverly Hills location page
galleryAlt: ZO Skin Centre homepage with a facial treatment hero, a clinic locations grid, and practitioner profiles

scope: UX strategy · IA · UI · Design system · Prototyping
headline: Unifying four locations into one clearer experience for discovering treatments and booking care

chapters.heading: Four locations. Four separate experiences.
chapters.lead:
Each had its own navigation, its own copy of the services, its own practitioner pages. The main site was a fork that sent you to one of them.

The services were mostly the same. The structure was built around which clinic owned the page, not around what someone was trying to decide.

The visual system had drifted from ZO Skin Health too.

items.title: A fragmented experience
items.body: Finding which clinic offered a treatment meant leaving one site and starting again on another.

items.title: A system adrift from the brand
items.body: Components had diverged from ZO Skin Health. The centre read as a separate company.

chapters.heading: I wanted to bring everything back into one place.
From four location experiences to one platform
chapters.lead: The old main site couldn't answer one question about a treatment. Everything that mattered lived inside whichever location site you landed on, copied four times over.

chapters.heading: Organise the experience around what people are trying to do, not around how the business is arranged.

title: Ibadat
scope: Prayer times · Reminders · Silence mode · Dua reading · Settings
headline: A prayer app that fits the way you practise
summary: I designed Ibadat to give people more control over their daily prayer routine—from advance reminders and automatic silence to a dua reader they can personalise.
snapshotNote: 2025 · In development · Android beta published by the client

chapters.heading: More control, without a crowded interface
chapters.lead:
The client wanted more than a prayer-time display. People needed to choose when an alert arrived, how it behaved, and which prayers would automatically silence their phone.

Dua reading needed the same flexibility: browse by category, save favourites, and adjust the script, translation, and transliteration.

The challenge was to make those choices easy to find while giving the app a more elegant visual direction.

chapters.heading: ~2 billion Muslims worldwide
chapters.lead:
Pew Research Center estimated the worldwide Muslim population at approximately 2 billion in 2020. This is the wider community Ibadat aims to serve, rather than a count of its users.

Source: Pew Research Center, “Muslim population change,” published June 9, 2025; population reference year: 2020.

chapters.heading: Turning a detailed brief into distinct daily tasks
chapters.lead:
The client supplied a detailed brief, with references from Mawaqit and Quran Touch. I organised it around the tasks people return to: checking a prayer time, configuring an alert, reading a dua, and changing preferences.

Prayer times, notifications, and silence mode share one prayer area. The date, location, and next-prayer countdown stay above its tabs. Alert and silence icons beside each prayer make the current choices visible in the schedule.

Calendar and location shortcuts sit beside the information they change, while broader settings remain available from the main navigation.

images.alt: Ibadat prayer times with a countdown, local schedule, and separate tabs for prayer times, silence mode, and notifications.
images.caption: The schedule shows each prayer’s alert and silence state, with date and location shortcuts above it.
images.label: Prayer times

chapters.heading: A shared visual language across the app
chapters.lead:
I used pale backgrounds, blue accents, rounded cards, and restrained Islamic patterns to give the app a calm, recognisable character.

The Figma file includes a dedicated Components page. Repeated controls—from tabs and switches to icons and navigation—give the prayer, dua, and settings screens a consistent language.

Arabic text has its own space in the reading view, with transliteration, translation, and source information grouped beneath it.

images.alt: Ibadat Figma component sheet showing tabs, alert chips, segmented controls, buttons, checkboxes, switches, inputs, number controls, and a slider.
images.caption: The actual control variants from the Figma Components page.
images.label: Controls

images.alt: Ibadat Figma card sheet with a calendar and dua cards in default and favourite states.
images.caption: Shared cards keep Arabic, transliteration, translation, and source information together.
images.label: Cards

chapters.heading: Decide when the phone alerts you—and when it stays quiet
chapters.lead:
Fajr is not one reminder for everyone. The brief separated waking for prayer, the last part of the night, suhoor, and an Imsak alert for someone already awake. I kept those purposes distinct instead of asking one alarm to cover them all.

Each reminder combines its timing with an alert choice: None, Silent, Vibrate, Beep, or Sound. “None” turns the notification off; “Silent” still delivers a message. The expanded controls appear beneath the reminder being edited.

Automatic silence has its own view, with a switch for each prayer. A person can keep the reminders they need and choose separately when their phone should stay quiet.

images.alt: Ibadat notification screen with separate reminder timings for Fajr routines and the other prayer times.
images.caption: Four separate Fajr reminders cover prayer, night worship, suhoor, and Imsak.
images.label: Reminder timing

images.alt: Ibadat Fajr reminder set to five minutes early, with None, Silent, Vibrate, Beep, and Sound options.
images.caption: Timing and behaviour expand within the selected reminder; None and Silent have different purposes.
images.label: Alert behaviour

images.alt: Ibadat silence mode with individual toggles for Fajr, Duhr, Asr, Maghrib, and Isha.
images.caption: Enable automatic silence for individual prayers.
images.label: Automatic silence

chapters.heading: Make automation visible—and provide a way back
chapters.lead:
When silence mode is active, the Home screen shows a status card with an “Okay” action to return to normal mode. This gives people a visible way to undo the change.

A separate “Notification not received” screen addresses another practical part of the brief: device battery restrictions can interfere with reminders. It explains the checks in order and provides shortcuts to battery optimisation and power management settings.

images.alt: Ibadat Home screen showing Silence mode is now active, an Okay button to return to normal mode, and time-based ritual guidance cards.
images.caption: The active state names what changed and keeps the return-to-normal action visible.
images.label: Silence active

images.alt: Ibadat notification troubleshooting screen with explanations and shortcuts to battery optimisation and power management settings.
images.caption: Troubleshooting links the app’s reminder settings with the device settings that may affect delivery.
images.label: Notification help

chapters.heading: Match local prayer times, one step at a time
chapters.lead:
Calculation settings begin with a clear order: check location, review Fajr and Isha, then Asr, Maghrib, and any remaining corrections. The screen explains that automatic settings may need to match a local mosque or religious authority.

The correction view shows an adjustment beside the prayer time it affects. Its Maghrib explanation calls out a specific dependency: sunset also informs the Hijri calendar and other features.

Hijri correction is a separate control, with a small −2 to +2 day range, an explicit Save action, and a date conversion view. Adjusting the calendar date stays distinct from changing prayer calculations.

chapters.heading: Dua reading, on your terms
chapters.lead:
The client scoped the reader around Hisn al-Muslim invocations. Categories such as Prayer, Travel, and Morning & Evening help people start with the situation they are in; favourites provide a way back to the duas they use often.

The reading view keeps Arabic, transliteration, translation, and the source together. Audio, editing, and favourite controls sit close to the text, so the reader can act without leaving the dua.

chapters.heading: Let people shape how they read
chapters.lead:
Reading preferences separate Arabic size from translation and transliteration size. People can choose the script and font, then show the reading layers they need. These controls are available in a sheet beside the reading experience.

Editable transliteration was a specific client requirement. I paired the text field with audio, speed, and repeat controls, so someone can listen while adjusting their pronunciation text, then choose Save or Cancel.

chapters.heading: Guidance for the moment, with sources to check
chapters.lead:
The Home design groups ritual guidance into Now, Weekly, Monthly, and Yearly views. The Sources feed uses the corresponding Daily, Weekly, Monthly, and Yearly groups for the supporting Quran and Sunnah material. Guidance and its evidence have distinct places in the app.

Settings bring language, number and time formats, and theme choices together. Home, prayer, and dua preferences remain separate, with links such as “Facing incorrect prayer time?” leading people towards the relevant help.

chapters.heading: In development, with an Android beta
chapters.lead:
The client has published an Android beta on Google Play, and development is continuing.

The ambition is to make daily worship easier for millions of Muslims through an app they can adapt to their routine. The beta is an early step towards that goal; reach and impact have not yet been measured.

The design brings prayer schedules, configurable reminders, automatic silence, and personalised dua reading into one app. The useful work was making that flexibility understandable: separate controls, consistent patterns, and reading preferences close to the content.
